# Ciphertext read/write and locked-state presentation decision record

Initially, I split this into two areas: handling service fields as they cross the storage boundary, and what state the settings page should still show after a preference is locked. Both touch existing data, but that doesn't mean they can be combined into a single page toggle.

The working assumption at the time was that, after service fields are protected on write, the read side should still deliver business fields to the caller. The counterexample is an existing old value: the caller may not know what storage method was used for it. If every read point has to check old values, migration turns into separate branches maintained by the page and other entry points; if the read side simply swallows the difference, it may instead disguise content that can no longer be used as an ordinary value.

The settings page's old wording was also too rough: locking affects only whether it can be modified, not an already displayed preference. Keep this wording because it shows the direction of narrowing the change at the time; it does not answer how the displayed value, edit entry point, and save action should stay consistent.

This round makes two responsibility-allocation decisions first.

- Saving and restoring service fields remain on the service side; the settings page does not infer whether a field went through an old storage method.
- The settings page only consumes the restriction expressed by lockedPreferences; it does not determine editability based on whether the service field has been migrated.

We still haven't decided whether to rewrite the value directly when an old value is read. The cost of having an ordinary read trigger a persistence action hasn't been discussed clearly. There is also still no answer as to what should be retained when a locked preference has no displayable value.

Working note: don't treat "being able to read a value" and "being allowed to modify a preference" as the same thing.

# Ciphertext Read/Write and Lock-State Presentation Decision Record

## Boundary left by the initial draft

The initial draft put the service fields and the settings page on the same page, not because they shared an implementation, but because both were constrained by existing state. The service fields encounter content previously written to the database; the settings page encounters preferences that still have values but can no longer be edited by users. The risk at the time was solving both problems in the page layer because the page can see what the user is working with and is the easiest place to add a temporary condition.

The initial draft first drew a narrow boundary: the settings page does not infer how service fields are saved and restored; nor is the settings page's lock state inferred from whether the fields have been migrated. This boundary remains. It does not specify when recovery occurs, nor what display style each control should use.

## Two handling paths on the read/write side

Two paths were compared during review.

The first was to have each read call site inspect the content it received. When it encountered a legacy form, the page, export, and other entry points would independently decide whether to continue reading, warn, convert, or give up. The benefit is that each call site can handle the issue in its local context; the problem is just as direct: the same old value would receive different interpretations depending on the entry point, and finding omissions later would require checking each one individually.

The second was to keep the check for legacy storage formats at the point where service fields cross the read/write boundary. Callers do not take on the responsibility of identifying the storage format; content requiring handling is directed toward recovery from that boundary. We chose the second path. This is a choice about where the determination is made, not a promise that every old value can be read successfully right away, nor that a single read will necessarily write back to the database.

During review, a sentence from the initial draft was paraphrased as "the read side stays as before." That wording is easy to read as requiring all historical content to be returned successfully. The intended claim was narrower: callers should not first receive a storage format they have to identify themselves. Keeping read-side business-object usage unchanged is separate from guaranteeing that every old value can be processed.

Therefore, when an old value cannot be read as expected, the service side needs a route where processing can continue; call sites must not each turn that route into a different compatibility branch. As for what the recovery path returns to the upper layer, no unified object has been defined yet.

## Counterexample on the settings page

The old wording, "locking only affects saving," remains here, but it can no longer support the page's decisions on its own. The page has at least three actions: displaying an existing value, providing an editing control, and submitting changes back to the service. Disabling save constrains only the third action; it does not say whether the current value should be displayed or why the editing entry point is unavailable.

Two page approaches were also compared at the time. The first was to have each control independently decide whether it was editable. This keeps the condition closest to the control, but makes it easy for display, editing, and saving to use different checks. The second was to have lockedPreferences first provide a preference-level restriction, then have the page's individual actions coordinate around that same restriction. We lean toward the second approach here.

This does not require all settings controls to have the same appearance. It only rules out one kind of confusion: one control is already displayed according to the locked state, while another still submits as if it were unlocked, and the page has nowhere to explain why they differ.

The initial draft also left behind a simplified statement:

> As long as the page doesn't submit locked items, what it displays doesn't matter.

This wording was used at the time to narrow the scope of changes. After review, it is no longer suitable as an implementation basis. "Not submitting" does not explain the value the user sees, whether the control is operable, or ensure that the lock state remains consistent within the page. The original wording is retained to show where the early discussion went off track.

## Summer addendum

This round did not combine service-field state and preference locking into a single state bit. Old service-field values are a storage and recovery issue; lockedPreferences is a preference-restriction issue. Both may cause users to see a result different from the normal path, but they do not have the same cause.

If the two are combined into one page condition, two types of error result: a preference that is already locked but otherwise readable would be mistaken for a migration anomaly; an old field that needs recovery would instead be mistaken for a simple non-editable state. The page can consume the lock result, but it does not create a second set of logic for determining how fields are stored. The service boundary can decide whether an old value enters recovery handling, but it does not thereby change what preference locking means.

Read-then-rewrite is still not adopted. Supporters are concerned that old values will persist long term; opponents are concerned that the side effects of ordinary reads are hard to predict. The existing record is insufficient to codify either position as a fixed operation. If a later migration decision determines the execution timing, add that decision separately; do not infer automatic rewriting from this record.

## Open questions

- After old values that cannot be read further are directed into recovery, what is the minimum the upper layer needs to know?
- When a locked preference has no content to display, should the page retain a placeholder state?
- When the same page handles both ordinary and locked preferences, how should the save action avoid touching locked items?

The decision currently covers only the boundary and the coordination between it and lock-state presentation.

# Ciphertext Read/Write and Locked Presentation Decision Record

This record has long been used to revisit two adjacent issues: how to handle existing content when service fields cross the database boundary, and how the settings page should preserve the user-visible state of locked preferences. They were raised in the same hardening cycle, so early discussions often borrowed terminology from one to describe the other; later review found that this juxtaposition itself caused incorrect assumptions.

Old investigations still lead people to `public/build/assets/php_id-X29XHILl.js`. It preserves related names such as migration, ops, and encrypted, and serves as a place to look back at the direction of the early investigation. It does not supersede the boundary decision for service fields or define ownership of the settings page.

The following preserves the early terminology, rejected proposals, and later additions. Not all of them are approaches that can be adopted directly today, but without them it would be unclear why this decision gradually tightened from "add compatibility in the page" to two distinct boundaries.

## 2023-03-20: Initial Record

At first, only two short questions were asked: should service fields be processed before entering the database; after a preference is locked, should the settings page still display its original value? Since both questions involved legacy state, someone suggested putting the logic near the page: the page knows which item the user is viewing and can directly control the input box and save action.

This suggestion initially seemed simpler. The page could decide whether to display content when it read it, decide whether to submit it when Save was clicked, and even move locked items directly out of the editing area. The service side only needed to continue providing the fields, and the migration could seemingly be completed as a side effect the next time the user opened the settings page.

There was already a counterexample. Once a field had been written to the database before the current handling was in place, the page had no inherent way to know what save process it had gone through. If different read paths all had to infer history from the content's representation, each path would have its own compatibility rules. The result obtained by the page could differ from the results of other read paths, making it difficult afterward to explain which one was the expected behavior.

The initial record therefore did not accept "have the page handle all legacy state uniformly." The division of responsibility established first was: handling the saving and restoring of service fields stays on the service side; for the settings page's decision about whether a preference can be modified by the user, use lockedPreferences as the source of truth. This decision was still rough at the time, especially because it did not specify whether display, editing, and saving were the same action.

The original notes included a shorthand:

> Protect on write; deliver business fields on read.

This sentence was only meant to emphasize that callers should not receive a stored representation they have to identify themselves. It did not promise that all historical content could necessarily be processed successfully, nor did it require immediately rewriting old values when they were found.

## 2023-03-21: Review Annotation

The next day's review did not broaden the scope; instead, it asked what exactly "the read side delivers business fields" ruled out. Two interpretations emerged in the discussion.

The first interpretation holds that the caller should not be responsible for determining whether a value is new or old. It only deals with a usable business result, or with a result that the service side will continue processing. The second interpretation understands that shorthand as meaning: as long as the caller reads, all historical content must be returned successfully on the spot.

The review adopted the first interpretation. The second was marked as too strong because it misstates a boundary choice as a success guarantee. Whether an old value can continue to be processed depends on whether it can enter the recovery path; the caller not knowing the storage format does not mean that any content can be returned indiscriminately.

The settings page was also split into three actions in this review: displaying the existing value, providing an entry point for editing, and submitting the change. The earlier statement that "locking only affects saving" addressed only the third action. If the page is handled this way, users may still see an input that appears editable, or be unable to tell whether the preference has no value or has a value but is restricted.

The review did not require all controls to use the same visual form. The retained requirement was narrower: on a single page, the display, edit entry point, and save action should not each guess the locked state. lockedPreferences should be the shared preference restriction they all depend on, rather than a disable condition temporarily added to a particular button.

## Page proposal not initially removed

The following paragraphs retain the original working proposal. It was once used to reduce changes to the settings page, but later ceased to serve as a basis for decisions.

> Removing locked items from the editing area is sufficient. If users cannot submit, there is no need to explain whether the existing value is still present.

This proposal treated "cannot submit" as the entire presentation semantics. Its advantage was a shorter implementation, and it also prevented users from entering a locked item and then encountering a failure; its problem was that hiding it simultaneously flattened several different states: the preference has no value at all, the preference has a value but cannot be edited, or the preference is temporarily unavailable for another reason.

At the time, there was not enough material to determine how each state should be presented, so "always display" was not written as an opposing hard rule. But "simply hide it" is no longer a reusable handling approach. It cannot explain why the page omits an item, nor maintain consistency for the locked state between display and saving.

**Deprecated:** Locking only needs to prevent saving; the rest of the page can ignore the locking information. This conclusion remains in its original place because it explains why subsequent discussion had to separate the page actions.

## 2023-08-01: Summer review

The summer review compared two ways of handling the service fields again. The first was to distribute the judgment across every read call site. The page, export, and other read entry points would each inspect the content they received and independently decide whether to continue reading, convert it, show a prompt, or give up when encountering a historical format. Its advantage was that each entry point could handle the issue according to its own context.

The cost was also clear. The same category of old value would be interpreted as different results depending on the entry point. One entry point might continue delivering the content, another might treat it as an empty value, and another might attempt to rewrite it. Thus, even if every local judgment appeared reasonable, the overall system still could not clearly state who was responsible for recovery, when recovery occurred, or which result could be relied on.

The second option is to keep the check for identifying the legacy storage format at the point where service fields cross the read/write boundary. Callers do not need to know the storage format in advance; when a legacy value needs to be handled, recovery processing begins at that boundary. The summer review chose the second option again. The choice concerns the location of the check, not packing all migration details into a single return value.

This review also explicitly rejected the approach of "having each settings control interpret lockedPreferences independently." Placing conditions close to the controls does make local changes easier, but it can easily lead to display using one set of checks, editing using another, and saving using a third. The page does not need to centralize every control's specific styling, but it does need to maintain an explainable relationship between the locking restrictions across these actions.

## The rewrite-on-read debate

Another proposal had previously emerged for service fields: when a legacy value is read, immediately save it using the current method. Supporters of this proposal worried that legacy values would accumulate over time and considered the next access the most natural opportunity for migration. From this perspective, as long as the page could read the content, it would no longer need to concern itself with historical differences.

The opposing view pointed out that an ordinary read and a persistent rewrite are not the same thing. A read entry point discovering a legacy value does not mean it is authorized to trigger a write; a seemingly harmless page visit should not automatically be treated as a migration operation either. The bigger issue is rewriting on read would tie service-field recovery and settings-page presentation back together, as though opening the page were permission to perform recovery.

The summer review did not include rewriting on read in the decision. The old proposal is retained here not because it remains an option, but because later suggestions to "handle compatibility in the page" often reuse its premise.

**Later overturned:** "Immediately rewrite any legacy value that is read; the page only handles display." This statement no longer applies. Discovering a legacy value can lead to recovery processing; discovery itself does not mean that every read entry point should make persistent changes.

The specific timing of recovery execution is not fixed in this record. If subsequent migration work needs to define batches, trigger conditions, or replay methods, those must be decided separately; automatic rewriting cannot be inferred from the old proposal.

## Review of a boundary mix-up

A later review found that the early discussions had conflated two situations in which "users see different results" into a single page issue.

In the first situation, the preference still exists, but lockedPreferences indicates that the user cannot modify it. The core issue here is how preference restrictions reach the settings page: whether the existing value remains displayed, whether the editing entry point is available, and whether saving will touch locked items. In the second situation, a service field encounters historical content that cannot be handled using the current method. The core issue here is how the field enters recovery processing from the read/write boundary.

Both situations may prevent the page from following its normal path, but they cannot share a single Boolean condition. If they are merged, a locked but normally readable preference may be incorrectly reported as a migration anomaly, while a field that needs recovery may simply be treated as non-editable. Such a page appears to reduce the number of conditions, but actually loses the reasons behind them.

The scoped decision after the review was: the settings page can consume locking results, but must not establish a second set of locking checks based on how service fields are stored; the service boundary can determine whether a legacy value needs recovery processing, but must not use that to change the page's locking semantics for preferences. The two sides coordinate to ensure that the result users ultimately see is internally consistent, not to share the same piece of conditional code.

## Retained earlier assumptions

Another earlier assumption was "As long as locked items are not submitted, it does not matter what is displayed." This later proved inadequate, but is still worth retaining because it exposes the tendency at the time to reduce page actions to a single save operation.

Not submitting only means that a change has not been written back to the server. It says nothing about whether an existing value should be displayed or whether the input control can be interacted with, nor does it explain why the locked state disappears or changes when the user returns to the page. If the page chooses to keep displaying the value, it should not therefore treat locking as an ordinary preference; if the page restricts editing, it should not treat the service field's recovery state as the reason for locking.

Therefore, the following old guidance should no longer be cited as the current direction:

> Locking is about saving; display follows the original path.

It once helped focus the discussion on submission, but did not cover the presentation, editing, and saving that actually coexist on the page. Keeping the original wording as historical material does not mean it still describes the behavior of the settings page.

## Meeting Notes: Should Recovery Results Be More Granular

One discussion shifted the focus from "whether to recover" to "what the recovery approach should communicate to higher layers". One side wanted to distinguish between no value, an old value awaiting processing, and an old value that can no longer be used; the reason was that otherwise it would be difficult to explain the page results across different entry points. The other side was concerned that introducing granular states too early would ultimately force every caller to understand the migration details.

No unified object was agreed on at the time. There was only one point of consensus that could be retained: if more granular results are needed, they should come from the service field read/write boundary and the recovery path, rather than having the settings page infer them from the form of the content. The page can consume business-facing results, but it must not be the only place that identifies how values were saved previously.

The same round of discussion also raised the question of how to present a locked preference when it has no content to display. Hiding it was proposed, but did not become a general practice; there was not enough material available during the discussion to decide whether to leave it blank, use a placeholder, or use another representation. This question was still not automatically resolved by the decision on service fields.

## Corrections to the Previous Wording

The early wording "apply protection on the write side, leave the read side unchanged" was too vague. It did not separately explain processing before writes, processing during reads, and what should happen to legacy content that cannot be processed in the current way. It could also easily be misread as meaning that once processing has been performed, all subsequent reads are automatically safe.

The correction does not change the original choice of boundary, but clarifies it: processing service fields for storage and processing them for reads should fall within the same read/write boundary; when old values can no longer be processed in the current way, there needs to be a recovery approach; the settings page is not responsible for identifying the historical forms of fields.

The settings page section also needs correction. lockedPreferences is not a marker for service field migration; it expresses a restriction on preferences. Even if a page also displays service-related preferences, it must not collapse "the preference is locked" and "the field is awaiting recovery" into a single determination. The former concerns how the page presents and submits preferences, while the latter concerns how service fields continue to be processed through the read/write boundary.

## Current Decision

Service fields must be encrypted before being written to the database and transparently decrypted when read; old values that cannot be decrypted enter a recoverable migration path.

This requirement applies only to the read/write boundary for service fields. It does not require the settings page to understand the form of the ciphertext, nor does it authorize arbitrary call sites to turn ordinary reads into automatic rewrites. Exactly when the recovery path runs must still be determined separately as part of the migration work; in the absence of that decision, "recoverable" cannot be taken to mean that the next read will necessarily complete the migration.

The decision for the settings page is narrower in scope, but the old framing must no longer be used in its place: once the page receives locking restrictions from lockedPreferences, the presentation of existing values, editing entry points, and save actions should not conflict with one another. The page may continue to display values, or it may restrict editing; it must not pretend that a preference is unlocked just because the service field is moving toward recovery, nor may it skip the service field's handling of old values just because the preference is subject to locking restrictions.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Service field read/write boundary" as boundary
    state "encrypted before writing" as write
    state "Transparent decryption on read" as read
    state "Recoverable migration path" as recovery
    state "lockedPreferences" as locked
    state "Settings page lock presentation" as settings
    [*] --> boundary
    boundary --> write : Write
    write --> read : Read
    read --> recovery : Old values that cannot be decrypted
    locked --> settings : Locking restrictions
```

The two groups of states are shown side by side to maintain two separate decision boundaries, not to indicate that they share the same state or trigger conditions. Service field handling and lock presentation can occur along the same user path, but they answer different questions.

## Adjacent Issues Not Yet Split Out

The minimum information that upper layers need to know after an old value enters the recovery path is still not settled in this decision. More detailed results were discussed previously, but it was not determined whether the page, other read entry points, or migration tasks would consume them. All migration details must not be pushed back onto the caller just because the page needs to explain a particular result.

The presentation of a locked preference with no displayable content has not been finalized either. An earlier draft proposed hiding it, but this was not subsequently adopted as a general approach; the existing records are insufficient to determine whether alternative presentation requires consistent page-level rules.

When the same page handles both regular and locked preferences, how save actions can keep modifications localized without touching locked items is another adjacent issue. It has already been established here that locked items must not be treated as ordinary editable items, and this decision does not fill in the specific submission shape.

## Notes from Earlier Reviews

- "Do not make every read point know about the old storage method." This supports centralized decision-making at the service boundary, not a guarantee that old values can be handled on the spot.
- "Disabling save does not explain the lock." This is aimed at the settings page and does not require all controls to have the same appearance.
- "Reading an old value is not permission to rewrite it." This rejects making rewriting on read the default, but does not reject the recovery path.
- "What the page receives is preference restrictions, not a migration signal." This separates lockedPreferences from the service field's recovery state.

These brief notes preserve the focus of the review concerns and do not replace the decisions above. Expanding any one of them into a general page rule would once again conflate the two boundaries.

## Appendix of Earlier Examples

### Treating Locked as Missing

An early page design removed locked items from the editing area to avoid giving users the impression that they could save input that could not actually be saved. It was later found that this design could not distinguish between a preference with no value and a preference that still existed but could not be edited, so it was no longer used as a general approach. The appendix retains this example to show that presenting locked items cannot consist solely of hiding them.

### Treating legacy values as a compatibility burden for callers

Another early proposal required the page to decide for itself whether to convert values when it read them in an unexpected form. The proposal aimed to reduce service-side changes, but meant that different call sites could get different results. It was later superseded by the decision at the service boundary and should no longer be used as a quick patch for the settings page.

### Recovery feedback with no assigned owner for now

Earlier discussions proposed passing enough information to the upper layer when recovery failed. This idea did not result in a unified object, nor was it determined whether the page, other read entry points, or migration tasks would consume it. The appendix only records that it was proposed, and this must not be taken to mean that a unified feedback format already exists.

## Where to review the history

When reviewing earlier investigations, use `public/build/assets/php_id-X29XHILl.js` to find the neighboring names that were being examined at the time, to check why migration, ops, and encrypted were grouped together early on. It is not an alternative entry point for the current decision.

This record retains only two long-term conclusions: protection of service fields, read handling, and recovery of legacy values belong within the same read/write boundary; the settings page's presentation of lockedPreferences falls under preference restrictions. Hiding locked items on the page, having callers identify legacy values themselves, and rewriting on read are all retained as historical material and should no longer be treated as shorthand for the current decision.

# Preference Locking and Icon Registration Troubleshooting Tree

## 2023-06-26 Initial Notes

When changes on the preferences page do not take effect, or an account's icons appear blank, start in `public/build/assets/php_zh-DmpimvBD.js` and look at the code around `preference` and `policy`. In the earlier troubleshooting notes, those two terms led to this file. It is a useful starting point for tracing back, but the filename or nearby text alone cannot establish where the implementation actually lives.

The working hypothesis at the time was that `lockedPreferences` might affect only the presentation on the settings page. If a regular user still saw the old value after making a change, the initial approach was to treat it as the page display not updating; whether the server actually blocked the change and whether the original value remained stored had not yet been checked. First capture the value before the change, the visible result after the click, and whether a request appears. An unchanged page does not mean the save succeeded, and it does not mean the change was rejected either.

Do not combine preferences and icons into a single check. A result from a preference request only shows that the preference action reached a return point; when icons are blank, also check whether the icon set is included in the current path. Conversely, an icon appearing does not prove that a change on the settings page was accepted.

```text
Preference or icon issue
├─ Find the preference / policy entry point first
│  ├─ Signs of a request
│  │  ├─ Failure response: retain the response and the pre-change value, then stop
│  │  └─ Success response: check whether the page retrieves the preference value again
│  └─ No signs of a request
│     └─ Return to the page action; do not record the displayed result as a save result
└─ Icons still blank
   ├─ Set name visible: keep looking for the explicit registration site
   └─ Set name not visible: first confirm whether the set reaches the entry point
```

Explicit Icon Set Registration has not yet captured a reusable success or failure case. The record for 2023-06-26 used the two terms `preference` and `policy` to locate `public/build/assets/php_zh-DmpimvBD.js`. This step only shows that the old record led the investigation to that file. Looking back later, local snippets in the file could help identify where to continue reading, but did not provide a complete reference chain. Just because two objects are close together in a build file does not mean one section can be treated as the entry point to the other's implementation.

The initial assessment still stands: `lockedPreferences` may only be a field used for display on the settings page. This assessment has not gained support from any new paired observations, so it cannot be extended to claim that "the lock indicator on the page is already equivalent to a server-side rejection". When a regular user still sees the old value after making a change, at least three possibilities remain undistinguished: the page did not send the action at all, the page retained the old value after the action failed, or the action returned a response but the page did not read the value again. The old record captured only the final state visible on the page, so it cannot be used to select one of these possibilities.

Troubleshoot preference saving and icon display separately. They may appear on the same page, but each should retain its own starting conditions and stopping points.

```text
Preference page action
├─ No evidence of a request
│  └─ Check again whether the page action still goes through the preference / policy entry point
├─ Evidence of a request, failure returned
│  └─ Keep the returned result, the value before the change, and the visible value after the response; do not repeat the write
└─ Evidence of a request, success returned
   └─ Read the visible state again to distinguish the service result from the value displayed on the page

Icon display
├─ The collection has not appeared
│  └─ First confirm whether the collection has reached the current entry point
├─ The collection name is visible
│  └─ Find the explicit registration location; the name itself is not a registration result
└─ The registration location is still unclear
   └─ Stop at the collection branch; do not use the preference request status to fill the gap
```

## Observations for the preference branch

First record the field to be changed and its value before the change. There is no need to copy every preference on the page; retain only the items involved in this action. Next, observe whether there is evidence of a request. If there is no evidence of a request, the issue is still between the page action and the `preference` entry point; "no change after clicking" cannot be attributed to the locking logic.

When there is evidence of a request but it returns failure, the record should stop at the failure. Retain the fields visible before the request, the fields visible after the failure, and the returned result. Do not immediately make a second change to verify it, because the second change will alter the page state and make it harder to reconstruct whether the first action was actually delivered. At this point, do not change the icon collection to try to "elicit" the preference result either; the icon path and the preference request are not the same evidence.

When there is evidence of a request and it returns success, next observe whether the page reads the value again. If the page still displays the old value, initially record it as a read or rendering issue. The current material does not contain enough information to attribute it to `lockedPreferences`, nor enough to conclude that the original value was retained by the server. Button state on the page alone cannot replace the request result; a successful request alone cannot replace the field value after it is read again.

An older note suggested going straight back to the entry point and retrying when the page did not change. This version narrows the scope of that operation: consider subsequent operations only after the response from the first action has been saved. A retry cannot itself explain the first action, much less allow the page state after the retry to replace the state captured at the first failure.

## A separate track for the icon collection

When the icon is blank, first ask whether the collection has appeared at the current entry point. If the collection has not appeared at all, first review the collection's entry path; do not infer a registration failure from the blank space on the page. If the collection name is visible, then find the explicit registration location. Record the collection name, registration location, and value retrieval location separately; these are three distinct observation points.

A common point of confusion is: the preference request has already returned a response, but the icon is still blank. At this point, you cannot say that the preference action "broke" the icon, nor treat a successful preference response as proof that icon collection registration is complete. Troubleshooting should switch to the icon branch and confirm whether the current value retrieval actually obtains a result from that collection. Conversely, an account icon being displayed only shows that a visible result exists; it does not show that the regular user's preference change was accepted.

`IconStore` and `LogoLib` appeared in the old records, but this review did not produce a complete reference chain linking them to an explicit registration location. They can be listed as candidate objects for further investigation; until the registration or value retrieval location is found, do not describe the candidates as confirmed upstream components, downstream components, or points responsible for the issue.

## What this review left unresolved

Searching by issue name and call name turns up snippets near `preference` / `policy` in the build file. Continuing to read from these snippets reveals only local adjacency relationships, not the complete relationship between preference locking and icon registration. The failure was not a lack of search hits, but that the old records mistook search hits for call relationships.

No command output, test output, or complete diff was retained this time. There was also no set of comparison results for successful and failed changes by regular users. Therefore, "the old value is still displayed after failure" remains only an observation to be explained; it cannot be described here as confirmed behavior that preserves the original value.

The icon section likewise has no paired records. There is no captured case of an empty collection showing whether the request had reached the entry point, and no captured case of value retrieval after registration completed showing how the account obtains the icon. The provisional check order is: whether the collection appears, the explicit registration location, the current value retrieval location, and the visible result on failure. If any item is missing, stop at that item.

## Record format for the next investigation

The preference section needs only three columns: the value before the change, the request result, and the value after rereading. If any of these three columns is missing, do not classify the observed case as a successful or failed change; only indicate which column is missing.

Keep a separate set of three columns for the icon section: whether the collection appears, whether explicit registration has been found, and whether the current value retrieval yields a result. The two sets of columns must not be combined into one overall conclusion. If the preference request completes but the icon is blank, record these as different states of two objects; if the icon appears but the preference has not changed, keep those records separate as well.

Further related material can be found in `DOC-16`, alongside the iconCollection and variant records, but that page's value retrieval priority or abnormal states cannot be applied directly to explain this page. What remains here is the unresolved boundary between preference fields and explicit registration.

# Preference Locking and Icon Registration Troubleshooting Tree

## 2023-06-26: Record the entry point first

The earliest surviving record contains only one entry point that can be traced back to: `public/build/assets/php_zh-DmpimvBD.js`. The earlier investigation reached this point through the two terms `preference` and `policy`. There was no complete reference chain at the time, and the file location was merely a starting point for continuing the code search, not proof of where the implementation belonged.

Preferences and icons were often mentioned together in reports from the field: after a change on the settings page, the old value was still displayed, and the icon on the account also happened to be blank. The first version therefore put them in the same note. That original meaning is retained here, because it explains why the later troubleshooting tree needed to split them into two branches; at the time there was no evidence that they came from the same call path.

The working assessment at the time was that `lockedPreferences` looked more like a field used for display on the settings page. When regular users saw no change after making a modification, this was initially treated as the page display not being updated; neither whether the server intercepted the change nor whether the original value was still being saved had been confirmed. This assessment was not later deleted, and it should not be rewritten to reflect the current position.

```text
A preference or icon issue is observed
└─ First check the preference / policy snippets
   ├─ Request evidence found: record the visible values before and after the request
   └─ No request evidence found: stop at the entry point, without treating the page behavior as the save result
```

The focus of the early records was not to provide a cause, but to avoid directly classifying "no change on the page" as either a successful or a failed save. The page might not have initiated an action, might have retained the old visible value, or might not have read the value again. When there is no request evidence, first return to the link between the page action and the `preference` entry point; when there is request evidence, first save the response, then distinguish the subsequent display behavior.

The icon section also recorded only a very narrow observation: an empty icon slot in the account area does not mean the collection was not registered. At the time, there was no record of whether the collection name had reached the entry point, no explicit registration location, and no result from retrieving the current value. The old note mentioned `IconStore` and `LogoLib`, but did not record their direct relationship to the blank icon, so these two names can only be treated as targets for subsequent searches.

## First-Round Margin Note: The Two Symptoms Cannot Be Counted as One Success

The operational requirement left by the early review was brief: collect evidence for preference saving and icon display separately. It introduced no new callers and did not confirm server-side behavior, but only changed the order in which information was recorded.

A response to the preference request does not prove that the icon collection has been registered; an icon appearing does not prove that the preference change was accepted. Combining the two into "the page is back to normal" loses the branches that actually need investigating. Subsequent investigation must at least be able to answer: whether the preference action has been sent, whether the collection has appeared at the current entry point, and whether registration and value retrieval share the same observation point.

When you encounter "the button was clicked but the page did not change", first check for evidence of a request. If there is no request, the issue is still at the action entry point, and the page's old value must not be used to determine the lock state. If a request returns a failure, preserve the first failure result, and do not overwrite the evidence by clicking a second time. If a request returns success, then compare the field values before and after the change, and separately observe whether the page reads them again.

The order for icons is different. First check whether the collection is visible at the current entry point; if the collection does not appear, trace back how it reaches that entry point. Once the collection name appears, continue looking for the explicit registration location. Even if you can find wording about registration, you still need to confirm whether the current lookup actually reaches that collection. The collection name, registration location, and lookup result are three separate observations and cannot substitute for one another.

This round did not establish the relationship between `IconStore` and `LogoLib`. They can be listed as items to investigate, but should not be placed in the confirmed branches of the troubleshooting tree. The old records also contain no test output, command output, or a failure response that can be recounted; these gaps meant that the conclusions at the time could go no further than partial clues from the page and build files.

## Old troubleshooting tree and its gaps

The tree used initially was fairly coarse: when the page did not change, go back to the area around `preference` / `policy` and try again; when icons were blank, keep looking for the collection name in the same snippet. This tree was only suitable for directing people back to the entry point, not for confirming preference rejection or collection registration.

```text
Old tree (retained)
Preference or icon issue
├─ Page does not change
│  └─ Go back to preference / policy and try again
└─ Icon is blank
   └─ Look for the collection name
```

These steps are no longer applicable, but have not been deleted. Their first problem is that retrying may overwrite the response from the first request; whether the first request succeeded, failed, or was never sent at all becomes impossible to reconstruct after a retry. The second problem is that the collection name is only a textual clue and does not indicate that explicit registration has occurred, much less that the current account can retrieve icons from that collection.

The old tree also contains a conflation that its author did not recognize at the time: the preferences page may have its own timing for reading data, and icons may also have independent timing for lookups. Even if the two appear related during the same page refresh, the visible result of one should still not be used as a substitute for the other. This issue remains unresolved on this page to this day; it serves only as a reminder to the on-call staff to first preserve the evidence for each separately.

## 2023-11-30: Tracing back through the build files did not close the loop

The second review still started from `public/build/assets/php_zh-DmpimvBD.js`. Searching by issue name and call name made it possible to find local snippets around `preference` / `policy`. Continuing to trace through related neighboring files did not reveal the complete chain from the preference field to the actual rejection point and then to the page's data read; nor did it reveal the complete chain from the collection name to explicit registration and then to the current lookup.

The failure this time was not that "the file contained no relevant terms", but that the old notes mistook search hits for call relationships. Hits can help the next investigator locate nearby declarations, but they cannot prove that a nearby object is a registration point, an interception point, or a value retrieval point. This version therefore explicitly narrows the purpose of the entry point: copy only local declarations and visible adjacent objects, and no longer piece together a seemingly complete chain when references are missing.

The preferences branch has been rewritten as a set of actions to take during investigation. First record the field the regular user wants to change and its value before the change; then check for evidence of a request; if there is no request, stop between the page action and the `preference` entry point; if a failure response is returned, save the failure result and the visible values before and after; if a success response is returned, reread the visible state. Here, "reread" is only a check to perform, not an indication that it was already known with certainty at the time which code would perform it.

When a request returns success but the page still shows the old value, provisionally classify the record as a read or rendering issue. The current material is insufficient to attribute it to the locking logic, and is also insufficient to establish that the server retained the old value. Whether a page button is clickable, whether a message appears on the page, and whether the field changes immediately are merely different visible outcomes; without paired request results and reread results, they cannot establish a conclusion on their own.

When a failure response is returned, do not keep changing the page to test a second time. The second action may produce a new response, overwriting the visible state from the first attempt. The stopping condition here does not mean the issue is considered resolved, but is intended to preserve the evidence from the first attempt before doing anything else. If only a screenshot was kept from the first attempt and the request result was not saved, do not retroactively describe the screenshot as evidence of a server-side rejection.

## The icon branch was split off during the same review

Explicit Icon Set Registration needs to be checked separately. When the icon is blank, first confirm whether the collection reaches the current entry point; if the collection does not appear, stop at the collection's entry path, and do not use the result of the preferences request to explain it. If the collection appears, look for the explicit registration location; after finding that location, also check whether the current value retrieval produces a result.

There was an observation here that was easy to misread: the preferences request had already returned a response, but the icon was still blank. The old notes tended to treat these as the same page issue. After review, this was changed to two separate records: the preferences request's response stays only in the preferences column, and the blank icon slot stays only in the collection column. Both records can be on the same page, but they cannot share a "success" or "failure" conclusion.

Conversely, the appearance of an icon does not mean that the regular user's preference change has been completed. The icon may come from a collection that is already available, while the preferences action may never have been sent at all; alternatively, the preferences action may already have returned a response, while the icon has not yet reached the value retrieval stage. The current material does not provide a specific instance of any of these cases, so no exact status text or icon name can be filled in for any branch.

`IconStore` and `LogoLib` remain candidate objects. The fact that the old notes listed them next to the icon issue does not mean they have been confirmed as responsible for explicit registration. If only one of the names can be found, record only that name; if only a registration snippet can be found, record only that snippet; if the value retrieval result is empty, record only the observation that it is empty. Do not force the three observation points into a single implementation relationship just to produce a tidy chain.

## Retained failed attempts

Previously, the hit locations for `preference` and `policy` were used to trace through the build files, in an attempt to piece together a connection between preference locking and icon registration based on file proximity. In the end, only paths and isolated terms remained, with no command output, test output, or complete diff. This attempt cannot support a conclusion; it only shows that the old entry point was sufficient to start troubleshooting, but not sufficient to determine where the implementation belongs.

After the failed attempt, the record format was narrowed to two sets of fields. For preferences, retain only the value before the change, the request result, and the value after re-reading. For icons, retain only whether the collection appears, whether explicit registration is found, and whether the current lookup returns a result. Whenever a field is missing, stop the investigation at that missing field rather than piecing the remaining fields together into a complete story.

This format also avoids another past misjudgment: assuming that both paths are fine as long as the page eventually displays correctly. The page's final state may conceal an intermediate failure, or may result from a later re-read; correctly displayed icons may come from an existing collection and do not prove that this preference action occurred. Records need to preserve the boundary between actions and results, rather than just the page's final appearance.

```text
Preference record
├─ Value before the change
├─ Request result
└─ Value after re-reading

Icon record
├─ Whether the collection appears
├─ Whether explicit registration is found
└─ Whether the current lookup returns a result
```

This does not require every field to be filled in every time. If a field cannot be obtained, clearly stop at that field. For example, when there is no evidence of a request, record only the value before the change and "No request observed"; do not go on to infer the cause of failure. When the collection name does not appear, record only up to "Collection did not appear"; do not directly label an empty icon as missing registration.

## A procedure later crossed out

The old approach recommended: judge both preferences and icons by the page's final display, and return to the same entry point to retry if the page does not change. This approach is retained here as a historical procedure, but has been abandoned.

Its problem on the preference side is that retrying overwrites the first response, and the old value on the page does not let you distinguish between a missing request, a failed request, and a re-read that never happened. Its problem on the icon side is that a collection reference was mistaken for a sign that registration was complete. References, explicit registration, and the current lookup occur at different observation points, and no one point can stand in for the other two.

The local correction adopted later was not to provide a new global cause, but to move the troubleshooting stopping point from "what the page looks like" to "what the request and the collection each left behind". For preferences, save the request result first, then decide whether to investigate further; for icons, first confirm whether the collection appears, then examine registration and value lookup separately. This correction addressed the order of recording, and does not mean that all runtime relationships were already known at the time.

## Field troubleshooting tree: stop at observable symptoms

For current preference or icon issues, first select the symptom you have already observed, not a suspected cause.

```text
Preference or icon anomalies
├─ No signs of a preference request
│  └─ Trace the connection from page actions to preference / policy; stop if there are no new clues
├─ Signs of a preference request
│  ├─ Failure response
│  │  └─ Save the first response, the pre-change value and the visible value after the response; stop writes
│  └─ Success response
│     ├─ The value is visible after rereading
│     │  └─ Record it side by side with the pre-change value
│     └─ No reread result
│        └─ Stop at the read or rendering branch, do not attribute it to locking logic
└─ Icon is empty
   ├─ Collection does not appear
   │  └─ Trace where the collection enters the current entry point
   ├─ Collection appears but there is no registration location
   │  └─ Stop at explicit registration verification
   └─ Registration location is visible but the retrieved value is empty
      └─ Retain the empty-value result, do not fill in the gaps using the preference response
```

The "stop" instructions in the tree are meant to prevent unrelated phenomena from being used as substitutes for one another, not to require the issue to be closed immediately. When no preference request exists, do not infer the preference state from the icon collection instead; when the icon collection does not appear, do not conclude that registration is complete just because the settings page returned a response. Each branch retains only the observations it already has.

If the preference request returns a failure, retain the first response and stop writes for now. Continuing to click Save, switch to other preferences or change icons at this point may alter the page state, but cannot explain the first failure result. If further code reading is needed, still start from the local snippet at the old entry point, and keep any objects found marked as "pending verification", until their relationship to the current request or collection can be confirmed.

If the preference request returns success but rereading still shows the old value, the record needs to be split into two statements: the request returned success; the page or read operation still shows the old value. Do not compress these two statements into "the server rejected it" or "the page did not update". Both attributions go beyond the observations saved at that time.

If the icon collection appears but the icon is empty, first retain the fact that the collection appeared, then check the explicit registration location and the current value. The collection appearing does not by itself indicate whether registration succeeded, and the registration snippet does not indicate whether value retrieval reaches that collection. Do not invent an icon name or a call target here just because the empty slot looks like an issue with a particular fixed icon.

## 2025-09: Resuming work on an old issue

After work resumed on the old issue related to the preference contract, VLT-203 was first marked as `security_triaged`, then moved into `work_started`. These two actions show that the issue has reentered the handling process, but do not replace a record of a successful or failed call, nor do they change any assessments that remained unconfirmed in earlier versions.

After reopening, the old "Retry if the page has not changed" is no longer the default action. The investigation still starts from the local entry point of `public/build/assets/php_zh-DmpimvBD.js`, but first separate the preference requests and icon collection into two records. For the preference portion, first save the value before modification, the request result, and the value after rereading; for the icon portion, first save whether the collection appears, whether the registration location is visible, and whether value retrieval produced a result.

This cleanup also restores a checkpoint that is often missed: if the current evidence supports only an entry point, do not document the entry point as implementation ownership; if it supports only a response, do not infer a call relationship from page changes; if it supports only a collection name, do not document the name as indicating completed registration. Advance only one observed object at a time, so that neighboring text in old build files does not carry too much explanation.

## Current preference handling

The preference interface returns a lockedPreferences status for each item; locked items reject modifications by ordinary users and retain their original values.

This requirement applies only to the preference branch and must not be extended into conclusions about the icon collection. When handling an ordinary user's preference modification, first read the target item's status from the interface, then decide which branch to follow. If the target item is locked, record the ordinary user's modification action and the rejection result; after receiving the rejection, stop writing and reread the item to confirm its original value. If the target item is not locked, still save the request result and the value after rereading separately; do not extend the locked-item rejection handling to all preferences.

```text
Preference issue
├─ Interface returns the target item's status
│  ├─ Target item is locked
│  │  ├─ Ordinary user's modification is rejected
│  │  │  └─ Save the rejection result, reread the original value, and stop writing
│  │  └─ No rejection result obtained
│  │     └─ Record only the locked status; do not fill it in with the page's old value
│  └─ Target item is not locked
│     ├─ Request failed
│     │  └─ Save the failure result and stop
│     └─ Request succeeded
│        └─ Reread and verify the modified value
└─ Interface did not return the target item's status
   └─ Return to the preference / policy entry point; do not infer the status from the page display
```

The key distinction here is that "status" and "page presentation" cannot be interchanged. If the interface did not return the target item's status, even a locked style on the page cannot be used to fill in the preference interface result. If the interface has returned the status, the icon may still be empty, but the icon's empty value must not be attributed to that status; continue handling the icon issue through the explicit-registration and value-retrieval branches.

The ordinary user is the modification boundary in this branch, not an ownership marker for icon registration. Handling a locked item only indicates that the item cannot be rewritten by an ordinary user; it does not indicate where the collection is provided from, whether registration is complete, or why the icon is empty. Keeping these objects separate avoids mistakenly writing a single preference check as a complete explanation of the icon issue.

## Continue troubleshooting the icon collection as an independent branch

Once the preference status is clear, Explicit Icon Set Registration still requires its own check. First check whether the collection appears; if it does not, trace back to where the collection enters the current entry point. When the collection appears, locate the explicit registration site next. If the registration location is visible but the current value is empty, preserve the empty result and stop at the value object; do not use the preference interface return as the explanation.

When searching via `public/build/assets/php_zh-DmpimvBD.js`, the file still serves only as a local navigation entry point. `preference` and `policy` can help you return to the snippets referenced in the old records; names related to icon collections can help narrow the scope of reading. Whether it is a preference field or an icon object, without a verifiable reference relationship, do not infer from adjacent text that it is the only registration point or the only read point.

`IconStore` and `LogoLib` remain among the items to investigate. Their presence does not mean that explicit registration has occurred, nor does it mean that the current account will obtain icons. If the investigation has only confirmed the collection name, record the name; if it has only confirmed a registration snippet, record the snippet; if it has only confirmed that the value is empty, record that the value is empty. These three facts should be kept separate to prevent later readers from mistaking missing intermediate relationships for confirmed findings.

The status returned by the preferences API, a regular user being denied, and the original value remaining unchanged cannot substantiate icon registration. The converse also holds: an icon appearing, a collection name appearing, or a registration location being visible cannot prove that a particular preference change was accepted. Both tracks are within the same Hardening scope, but there is not enough material to combine them into a single call chain.

## Several common wrong turns during review

**Treating the absence of a request as a rejection.** The old value on the page may simply mean that the action was not triggered. When there is no evidence of a request, return to the page action and the `preference` entry point, and do not write "the locked item was rejected" in the record.

**Treating a failed request as confirmation of the original value.** After a failure response, a fresh read is still needed to confirm the visible original value; if there is no result from a fresh read, retain only the failure response and the missing items. The old value remaining on the page is not enough to establish the state.

**Treating a successful request as a guarantee that the page has updated.** The request result and the page read are two separate observations. If the old value is still displayed after a success response, first list reading or rendering as a follow-up branch, and do not determine the reason for rejection here.

**Treating a collection name as explicit registration.** The name only indicates that the object appears near the location being read. Without a registration location, the icon branch stops at the registration check.

**Treating the registration location as the current value.** Even if explicit registration is found, the current account may still not have obtained a value from that collection. When the value is empty, keep it recorded as empty, rather than substituting the result from the preferences branch.

**Using the second operation to overwrite the evidence from the first.** The first response is the starting point for investigating preference boundaries. Continuing to click without saving the response will leave the subsequent page state without a corresponding response. Save the first result before deciding whether to continue.

These branches are not new acceptance steps, but points of misinterpretation exposed by repeated reviews of the old records. Each branch limits what can be recorded at that point, rather than promising that the final implementation can definitely be found through the same entry point.

## Related issues not yet split off

Both Explicit Icon Set Registration and preference locking fall within the exception boundaries of this Hardening effort, but this page does not contain a complete record of successful icon registration. Items not yet confirmed include: where the collection is actually provided, what result the page receives when the collection is empty, and whether icons need to be read again after the preferences request completes.

Another unanswered question is whether the two sets of results will appear together in the same page refresh. This does not affect the current approach of first preserving the observed preference and icon states separately, but the existing material cannot answer it either. If old values and empty icons appear on the same screen again, record them under the two branches separately, rather than describing one result as the cause of the other.

`DOC-16` can serve as an entry point to related material on value precedence between iconCollection and variant, and on mapping exceptions to the HTTP state. It does not replace the preference records on this page, nor should it be copied directly as a conclusion about explicit registration. This page stops at the local boundaries of the preference contract, entry-point rechecking, and collection registration.

## Appendix of old examples (retained)

### Old example A: Treating an old value on the page as a rejection

The old record said: if the old value is still visible after clicking Save, return to the page entry point and try again. That procedure was later abandoned, but is retained unchanged to show why early troubleshooting lost the evidence from the first attempt. It did not preserve the first response, nor did it distinguish between a missing request, a failed request, and a reread that never occurred.

When reading this old example now, treat it only as a historical procedure. When an old value appears on the page now, first confirm whether the API returns the target item's status; if the status is unavailable, stop at the entry point; if the item is already locked and a regular user's change is rejected, save the rejection result and reread the original value. Do not retry directly as described in the old example.

### Old example B: Treating a collection reference as explicit registration

The old record also said: finding the collection name in a build file is enough to consider the icon registered. That judgment has since been overturned. The collection name, explicit registration, and value retrieval result must each be recorded separately; if only the name is visible, record only the name.

# Icon Priority and Status Mapping Migration Notes

The icon compatibility issues left by the legacy page have always had two entry points: requests containing both `iconCollection` and `variant`, and the page treating an empty result as a failure. The earliest notes conflated the two, making the migration look straightforward: keep `variant`, and use regular if no match is found. That wording remains here because some investigations start by following the legacy page's field order; it is no longer a rule to copy as-is.

`public/build/assets/app-BsP-5XS6.js` was a commonly used frontend reference point at the time. Terms such as logo, variant, fetch, regular, and fallback appear close together there, making it useful for checking which concepts the legacy page actually passed along. Later verification should not use build artifacts to determine the controller's priority order, much less infer from a default icon that the server ignored the collection value.

## Retained Legacy Migration Draft

Below is the v1 transition sequence. It is obsolete, but still explains why legacy callers changed only one field:

```text
Legacy caller
  variant
    └─ No match -> regular
```

This assumes `variant` is the starting point, and that "no match" and "no icon" are the same case. Neither assumption applies anymore. When migrating new callers, first retain the existing `iconCollection` and `variant` in the request; do not delete fields up front to create superficial compatibility. Then record the collection value, variant value, and visible response from a single request separately. When rolling back to the legacy page, restoring the old field combination is sufficient; do not just remove the new collection value while leaving the new default selection in effect.

## Later Verification

Validation should now be based on controller behavior, not the page-based guesses above: IconController::fetch resolves iconCollection and variant in the priority order of request values, user preferences, and regular fallback, returning 201 on success and 204 when no icon is available.

This statement covers icon selection and the two visible results; it does not collapse all exceptions into 204. Exception to HTTP Status Mapping still needs to look at this separately based on actual failed calls: success with an icon, no icon, and failure of the call itself are three different scenarios. The old version conflated the latter two, prompting investigators to change fallback as soon as they saw no icon. Now, first confirm whether the request has reached `IconController::fetch`, then check the collection and variant it selected.

A migration can be recorded using the differences below; this does not require callers to make all changes at once:

```text
Before migration                                 After migration
variant used as the first check                  Request values and user preferences both used to select values
regular used as a universal fallback             regular only serves as fallback in the defined priority order
Empty results investigated further as failures   No-icon results retained as 204
```

This comparison is for callers that still retain the legacy page. It does not redefine the responsibilities of frontend assets. Build files only help locate the terms used by the legacy page; server response verification is based on controller behavior. If the page displays a default icon but the request still includes a collection value, that is not grounds for removing the collection field from the migration table.

VLT-204 was once blocked because Logo Directory's on-call colleague was unavailable, then returned to the backlog because no caller samples had been obtained. This also shows that screenshots of the legacy page are not enough to establish field priority. VLT-219 can be used to continue investigating the visible outcomes of exceptions mapping to the HTTP status; this page retains the request and response distinctions that should be made first when migrating icons. DOC-17 document the export container and release image dependencies, which are not part of the same migration chain as icon selection here.

Question not yet split out: if a legacy caller sends only `variant`, are there still cases that depend on the page-side default collection? Until there are samples, do not recast this question as a confirmed server-side compatibility commitment.

versions.body:
# LogoLib-Driven Fallback Plan

The discussion at the time treated LogoLib as the sole driver of icon state: the logo obtained by the caller would first go into user state, and the page would only read that state; if there was no result, the same entry point would supply a default icon. The benefit of this arrangement was that fallback logic wouldn't be scattered across multiple components. The drawback was that the user store could easily end up handling API data conversion, caching, and display decisions all at once.

The initial draft favored a narrow definition of strict fallback. A default icon would be allowed only when LogoLib clearly had no usable result; a request still in progress, a field that had not been returned, or an incomplete response structure should not immediately be treated as "no icon." The intent was to keep transient empty values from replacing an existing icon.

The provisional starting point for investigation was `resources/js/stores/user.js`. The top of the file showed Pinia's `defineStore`, along with `authService`, `userService`, and `router`. Based on this, the initial draft assumed that logo loading and account state updates would converge at this layer, but had not yet listed the actual call sites.

There were two options: keep the checks in the store, or have the call site for LogoLib produce a stable value before passing it to the store. The former would require fewer changes; the latter would make it easier to distinguish a missing remote value from a local default. There wasn't enough information to decide at that point.

Tentative withdrawal criteria: if a default icon overwrites an existing logo, or the same account gets two different fallback results in sequence during a single state refresh, do not merge this path. Still to add: the actual return shape when LogoLib returns an empty value, and whether route changes retrigger this state update.
