# Public Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

This record preserves the boundaries of a discussion about maintaining the public entry point, rather than serving as an overall account of all subsequent release arrangements. At the time, the initial draft framed the issue as a choice between "keeping the current `release-runtime` entry point" and "adjusting the window"; this framing was useful because it preserved the action that actually needed a decision then, but it also compressed many coordination matters that had not yet been explored into the two Chinese characters for "window".

Following this review, the original decision remains unchanged: retain the existing entry point for this round, and do not schedule entry point changes in the same window. What has changed is that the rationale needs to be stated more narrowly. We did not establish that the old entry point was suitable for every scenario, nor did we establish that a change would necessarily cause a failure; all that could be confirmed at the time was that the existing material covered the current repository entry point and its outputs that could be reproduced through reruns, while the coordination information required for an entry point change was incomplete. If a change were approved directly on the basis of this limited material, the risk would not be that some implementation detail might be wrong, but that after the switchover, the parties involved would not be able to use the same record to explain what they should continue using or whether they could still fall back to the old entry point.

## Decisions Retained

- The existing `release-runtime` entry point will continue to serve as the public entry point for this round.
- Adjusting the window will not be bundled with this maintenance; it requires a separate arrangement that can be discussed.
- The old entry point will not be withdrawn for now. If a switchover is initiated later, the old entry point must remain available as a fallback during a clearly defined transition period, rather than disappearing as soon as the new arrangement appears.
- Any new change proposal must first document the actual impact that has already occurred or is expected, the person responsible for the handoff, and the conditions for withdrawing the old entry point. If any of these is missing, the conclusion remains to retain the entry point.

Here, "actual impact" does not simply mean whether a change will be troublesome. The discussion needs to address continuity of use of the public entry point, whether existing outputs can still be reproduced through reruns in the original way, and whether the people involved in the switchover can identify where they fit into the handoff. Without these descriptions, "adjusting the window" is merely a scheduling statement and cannot serve as the basis for a decision.

The initial draft's conclusion therefore remains valid, but it is a conservative decision, not an endorsement of the existing entry point's quality. The public entry point's continued existence only indicates that the evidence at the time was insufficient to support a change; it does not mean that the maintenance burden has disappeared, nor that every subsequent release should follow the same cadence.

## The Two Options Compared at the Time

| Approach | What could be relied on at the time | Reasons for rejection or retention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current entry point | The known entry point, invocation names organized around it, and outputs that could be reproduced through reruns | Keeps the old entry point on the public path, maintenance issues do not automatically disappear |
| Adjust the window and push forward with the switchover | There was an intention, but no complete description of the impact | The coordination roles, the method for withdrawing the old entry point, and the post-switchover rerun relationships had not all been settled together |

This comparison does not present "retention" as a cost-free option. The costs of retaining the entry point were already part of the discussion: the public entry point still needed maintenance, later users might still treat it as the default path, and the window adjustment would continue to be delayed. It was simply that those costs had not yet outweighed the cost of lacking a switchover record.

On the other hand, adjusting the window was not rejected as infeasible either. What was rejected was the approach of "including it directly in this round before the information was complete". If the three parts covering impact, coordination, and withdrawal can later be completed, the change can be discussed again; but that should be a new decision, and this old record must not be treated as approval already granted.

## A View Corrected During Review

Around the time of the initial draft, there was a less cautious view: entry point changes were mainly a matter of release cadence, and all that was needed was to free up the window. This understanding is no longer used following the review. A window only specifies when actions are scheduled, and cannot replace an explanation of the switchover itself. When a public entry point changes, what users see is whether the entry point is still available, whether the original reruns can still be performed, and who will handle the handoff if problems arise; none of this materializes simply because a window has been reserved.

This does not mean that every instance of entry point maintenance requires a lengthy plan. When the material covers only one existing entry point and a small number of outputs, the record should be limited to that scope as well. The issue is that moving from "keep it for now" to "change it now" requires not more abstract reasoning, but a few facts directly related to the switchover. Without those facts, retaining the old entry point is actually the more honest approach.

The decision path at the time can be condensed into the small diagram below. It reflects the threshold for this decision and should not be treated as a fixed process for every future release window.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Existing release-runtime entry point] --> B{Is the change record complete}
    B -- No --> C[Retain the entry point this round]
    B -- Yes --> D[Discuss the change separately]
    C --> E[Keep the old entry point available as a fallback]
    D --> E
```

"Complete records" in the diagram does not mean filling out every part of a generic form. For this discussion, it means at least that three things can be considered together: what the change will alter, who is responsible for bringing the relevant people into the new arrangement, and under what conditions it will still be possible to fall back to the old entry point. When the three are scattered across different communications, any one of them may appear to have been handled, yet it is still impossible to judge whether the switchover as a whole is under control.

## Why the Old Entry Point Was Not Immediately Withdrawn

The old entry point was not retained because it had been deemed the sole long-term entry point. Its role was to leave a fallback for coordination that had not yet been completed. If the change happens first, and it is later discovered that rerunning the outputs still depends on the original arrangement, or that one party has only received the old entry point, rollback capability becomes a matter of reconstructing what happened; trying to reconstruct who did what from memory at that point usually only makes maintenance of the public entry point harder.

Therefore, the phrase "an old entry point available as a fallback" in the initial draft retains its original meaning: the old entry point should not become invalid as soon as the switchover is announced. It needs to continue to exist until it can be confirmed that the new arrangement has been taken up. No fixed duration or automatic withdrawal conditions are given here, because the material available at the time did not establish those details. Turning an unconfirmed duration into a rule would make this old decision appear to be based on more information than was actually available.

The review also confirmed one point: the existence of the old entry point cannot itself serve as a coordination record. Someone still being able to access the old path does not mean the switchover is complete; conversely, the old path still being available as a fallback does not mean all users should remain on it. The state of the entry point and the state of the handoff must be documented separately. The initial draft did not spell out this distinction, making it easy for readers to misread "retention" as "no switchover preparation is needed".

## Scope of the Coordination Role

No individual names were fixed in this record for this round. What is needed here is a clearly defined coordination role: confirm that the impact description is complete before the change, handle questions about the old entry point during the switchover, and check for situations that still require rollback before withdrawal. This role can be assigned through subsequent detailed arrangements, but someone cannot be sought out for it on an ad hoc basis after the entry point changes.

There is also a practical reason not to fix names: this material covers maintenance of the public entry point itself, not staffing schedules. Equating someone who participated in the discussion at the time with the long-term owner would mistake participation in a single meeting for an established assignment of responsibility. What must be established is that someone will handle the handoff, not that an outdated staff list is created in this old decision.

The person in the coordination role should receive more than a generic "please keep an eye on the switchover". At a minimum, they should see the scope of the entry point change, the current state of the outputs that can be reproduced through reruns, the reasons for retaining the old entry point, and where to return for further discussion if withdrawal is delayed. Without this information, the coordinator can only relay the conclusion, not judge whether it can still be carried out.

## Objections Still Retained

The objection to retention has not been removed. It pointed out that once the public entry point remains in place, subsequent maintainers will tend to keep relying on it, and the window adjustment will keep being pushed back because there is no clear trigger. This is a reasonable concern, especially once the entry point's name has become the default way of referring to it. Continuing to retain it will not stop maintenance costs from accumulating.

However, at the time, the objection did not provide enough switchover material to replace the conservative decision. It explained "why it should not be retained indefinitely", not "how to change it safely now". The two cannot substitute for each other. Keeping them side by side is intended to prevent later readers from mistakenly thinking that no one raised the costs of delay at the time, and to prevent this record from being read as permanent approval of the old entry point.

One issue also remains unresolved: outputs that could be reproduced through reruns were used as evidence at the time, but their specific relationship to subsequent entry point changes is not elaborated on this page. The review did not try to fabricate that relationship. Anyone preparing a new change on this basis should first document which outputs must be preserved, then discuss the window; they must not infer that the post-switchover path is also ready merely because "rerun results already exist".

## Relationship to the Handoff Record

The details of the switchover actions are kept separately in DOC-44. The steps from that material are not reproduced here: this page only records why the change is not being included in this round's maintenance window, and why the old entry point must be kept available as a fallback. The relationship between the two pages should not be understood in reverse, either. DOC-44 can help organize the handoff, but it cannot automatically change the deferral decision already made on this page; changing the entry point still requires a fresh assessment of whether the impact, coordination, and withdrawal conditions are complete.

This decision is still cited because it preserves the reasons for not expanding the scope of the change at the time. It is no longer an operating guide for new windows. If later discussions continue to cite it, they should also recognize the gaps it leaves: the entry point may continue to be retained, but coordination cannot therefore be omitted; the old entry point may exist temporarily, but that does not mean its withdrawal conditions can be left unwritten.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance Discrepancy Review

This records a discrepancy during a maintenance window for the team's public entry points. The observed result did not match the original plan. The initial record captured the impact, temporary recovery, and what was still unconfirmed about the cause; temporary recovery must not be written up as though the root cause had been established.

## Incident Timeline

- Initial detection: While the maintenance window was in progress, the result from the public entry point did not match the plan agreed at the time. Initially, all that was confirmed was that "a discrepancy had been observed"; the impact was not recorded separately by entry point, consumer, and time period.
- Further checks: The first check on site was whether the entry point was still usable, followed by a review of the original plan. The checks did not produce a complete chain of evidence sufficient to explain the source of the discrepancy. Later checks traced `public/build/assets/OAuth-BLvs4XQK.js` and the call name used at the time; that location could only serve as a search lead and could not, on its own, show where the maintenance action had actually taken effect.
- Temporary recovery: A rollback was performed using the retained old entry point. The public entry point then returned to a state where processing could continue. "Recovery" here means the observed result was usable again, not that the relationship between the original plan, the old entry point, and the actual result had been established.
- Before the window closed: The rollback drill sheet was also reviewed. It had focused more on whether the actions could be carried out; only this time were the actual impact, the coordinator, and the old entry point that could be withdrawn added to the record.

## Impact

The clearest impact at the time was that, during the maintenance window, the result the team saw from the public entry point did not match the original plan, and a temporary rollback was needed so work could continue on site. The initial draft left no verifiable record of which callers were affected or how long the discrepancy lasted. Therefore, "recovered" cannot be taken to mean that every entry point was unaffected, nor can the impact scope be expanded to cover entities that were not observed.

## Assessment at the Time

The early response focused on whether the entry point had been switched back. That could help restore operation on site first, but it did not answer why the discrepancy occurred. Later reviews based on the file location also did not yield enough material to narrow the cause down to a particular code change or a particular fixed entry point. The earlier assessment is retained here: rollback was an effective on-site response, not a conclusion about the cause.

## Retained Control Points

The rollback drill sheet needs to record three things together: what the actual impact was, who is responsible for coordinating information from the scene, and how the old entry point can be withdrawn. In particular, when the old entry point can still be used for temporary recovery, a way to withdraw it must be retained; recording only "recovered" is not enough. This page did not go on to detail specific forms or check commands at the time; those gaps should not be filled in to create a new on-call process.

## Unconfirmed Items

It remains unconfirmed whether the discrepancy was caused by the maintenance action, a change in entry point state, or the interaction between the two. It is also unconfirmed whether the impact covered all public entry points. If this is revisited later, first compare the original plan, the actual observed result, and the rollback drill sheet, then decide whether there is enough evidence to amend this old record.

# Public Entry Maintenance FAQ

This page preserves the three questions that keep recurring in public entry maintenance. They all appear to concern the same entry, but actually point to different actions: confirming an existing path, withdrawing a candidate path, and deciding whether the version can be closed out.

At the time, we also inspected resources/js/services/systemService.js under the call name release. This location only helps people find records near the entry; it is not permanent ownership of the candidate path, nor does it turn the three questions into a single source-code question.

## What can the existing release-runtime entry prove?

It can prove that the team already has a findable public entry and that the successful path associated with the entry was once seen or recorded. It cannot, by itself, prove that the candidate path is still valid or that the failure boundary and recovery action have been verified. The entry being visible and the path being traversable still do not, by themselves, establish that maintenance is complete.

Entry records are useful for locating a successful path that has already been followed, but not as a basis for closeout. One person being able to find the entry and another engineer being able to confirm the result through the same entry are two different things; the old records stop at the first.

Early records grouped the entry and the successful path together, assuming that a visible entry and a traversable successful path were enough to close the maintenance item. This old guidance is retained in the historical materials because it explains why the work was handled that way at the time; the subsequent review only narrowed the conclusion to the entry and successful path and did not supply any validation that was not recorded. If only a successful path is beside the entry, the status of the candidate path cannot be inferred from this location.

This is also why the later review did not turn "entry exists" into an ownership conclusion. The review only narrowed what the entry can establish; it did not add evidence that the candidate path is still usable, how failure would manifest, or that recovery is complete.

## Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?

There is currently no owner we can verify. The withdrawal action cannot be assigned directly to the entry maintainer just because the candidate path appears near the public entry; likewise, the proposer cannot be assumed responsible for withdrawing it solely because the path was proposed. On this page, maintaining the entry and withdrawing the candidate path are two separate actions.

The withdrawal question is who performs the removal when the candidate path is no longer retained; it is not the same as asking who maintains the public entry. The old guidance does not describe the handoff between the two, nor does it say whether a path automatically transfers to one party once it has been proposed. Filling the gap with "handled by the entry side" would add an unsupported judgment beyond what the old records say.

What is missing here are targeted rerun records and records that tie the withdrawal action to a specific maintenance assignment. Without these materials, the answer remains unknown. The issue "targeted rerun records are missing" can be logged, but a default team or the name of the existing entry cannot stand in for the owner.

## Under what conditions can it be closed?

The team's standing criterion is: "The work for the version is considered closed out only when another engineer can rerun the successful path, the negative boundary, and the recovery action." The successful path answers whether the path can be traversed, the negative boundary answers where it should not pass, and the recovery action answers how to return to an available state after a problem occurs.

Here, "rerun by another engineer" is not a matter of repeating the entry name; it means being able to separately reach a successful result, reject cases that should not pass, and complete recovery after a problem occurs. If any one of the three exists only as a verbal explanation, the closeout assessment is still incomplete.

The release-runtime entry can provide at most a clue for the first part; it cannot replace the other two. If only the successful path is added later, the entry description can still only be updated; the owner responsible for withdrawing the candidate path and the closeout determination remain unconfirmed. When targeted rerun records are missing, this can be logged as an issue, but the version cannot be marked as closed on that basis.

This page previously treated "the successful path is usable" as a closeout signal; that is exactly why it should be retained but not used as the current guidance. What can be retained now is the entry record and the unconfirmed items; they cannot be used to announce that ownership of the candidate path has been determined or that the version has been closed.
